name: Hybrid Search
question: How do I get meaning and exact matches together?
summary: Run dense (vector) and sparse (BM25) search side by side and fuse the two result lists, usually with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which combines ranks rather than raw scores. Add metadata filters for date, tenant and permissions so results are both relevant and allowed.
useCases: Queries that mix meaning with codes, names or jargon
When neither vector nor keyword search alone reaches your recall target

items.detail: exact terms via BM25 or SPLADE
applied before or after the vector search

steps: Index each chunk in both a vector index and a keyword index
Retrieve the top 50–100 from each and fuse with RRF
Apply permission and tenant filters before results leave the database
Re-rank the fused list and test on both kinds of query
pitfalls: Two indexes to keep in sync
Raw scores aren’t comparable across methods; use ranks or normalize
Post-filtering can leave too few results, so oversample or pre-filter
remember: Dense for meaning, sparse for words, fuse by rank.
caption: Documents found by both methods rise to the top. Scores are computed with k = 60.

comparison.best: Two indexes to keep in sync

code.text: docs = load_chunks()                   # each chunk: text, tenant, updated_at
bm25 = BM25Okapi([d.text.lower().split() for d in docs])
emb = model.encode([d.text for d in docs], normalize_embeddings=True)
allowed = np.array([d.tenant == user.tenant for d in docs])
for rank, i in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
fused = [i for i in rrf(top_d, top_s) if allowed[i]][:20]
order = np.argsort(-ce.predict([(query, docs[i].text) for i in fused]))

steps.title: Index every chunk twice
steps.text: A BM25 index for exact terms and an embedding index for meaning. Both use the same chunk IDs and carry the same metadata.

steps.title: Filter to what the user may see
steps.text: The tenant filter is applied before ranking, so every candidate is one this user is allowed to read.

steps.title: Retrieve from both
steps.text: Dense search ranks D3 first and D1 second. BM25 ranks D1 first, because it contains the exact code 809.

steps.title: Fuse ranks with RRF
steps.text: Each list adds 1 ÷ (60 + rank). D1 gets 1/62 + 1/61 = 0.0325 and D3 gets 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0323. Raw scores are never compared.

steps.title: Keep the fused top
steps.text: Documents found by both methods rise to the top; documents found by only one follow. The top 20 go forward.

steps.title: Re-rank and test both query types
steps.text: A cross-encoder orders the final few. Evaluate code-style and meaning-style queries separately, since each method fails on a different kind.

pros: Catches exact codes, names and jargon that embeddings blur
RRF needs no score normalisation to start
Robust across very different query styles
Tenant and permission filters fit naturally
cons: Two indexes to build, store and keep in sync
Raw scores are not comparable, so fusion needs care
Weighted fusion needs tuning for each domain
Post-filtering can leave too few results
avoidWhen: Queries are purely semantic, with no codes or rare terms
The latency budget cannot absorb a second retrieval

playgroundGuide.scenario: An IT service desk at a Mumbai bank runs a wiki search for engineers. Three typical queries are shown: one hinges on an exact error code, one says the same thing as the right page in different words, and one mixes both. Dense and BM25 scores are fixed; you choose how to combine them and where to apply the tenant filter.
controls: Choose one of the three queries.
Choose the fusion method, and set k for RRF or α for weighted fusion.
Choose no filter, filter after ranking, or filter before ranking.

outputs.name: Top 5 returned
outputs.meaning: The results the engineer sees, with scores; green is the right page, red a page from another tenant.

outputs.name: Rank of the right page
outputs.meaning: Where the page that answers this query lands.

outputs.name: Right page in top 3, all queries
outputs.meaning: How many of the three query styles this setting handles.

outputs.name: Pages the user may not see
outputs.meaning: Results from Finance or HR that should never reach this user.

presets.name: Dense only
presets.expect: The error-code query puts D4 at #5; 2 of 3 queries hit, and one Finance page leaks.

presets.name: RRF
presets.expect: D4 rises to #2 and all 3 queries hit, but D6 from Finance still leaks.

presets.name: BM25 only
presets.expect: The meaning-style query puts D2 at #4, and two pages from other tenants appear.

presets.name: Filter after ranking
presets.expect: No leaks, but only 4 of 5 results are left on the page.

practice.scenario: An internal IT wiki gets queries like “VPN error 809 on Windows”. Vector search finds VPN troubleshooting pages; BM25 finds the one page that mentions error 809. Reciprocal Rank Fusion puts the page that both methods found at the top.

industries.use: Natural questions mixed with error codes and product names
“running shoe size 9 model 41” mixes intent, size and model number
Scheme codes and ISINs alongside plain questions

practice.analogy: Asking two experts, one who knows the subject and one who knows the catalogue numbers, and trusting the answers they both give.

library.name: Weaviate (or any DB + RRF)
library.what: Weaviate runs vector and BM25 search in one hybrid query; RRF itself is ten lines if your database lacks it.

samples.code:
import weaviate

client = weaviate.connect_to_local()
wiki = client.collections.get("WikiPage")

res = wiki.query.hybrid(query="VPN error 809 on Windows",
                        alpha=0.5,      # 0 = keyword only, 1 = vector only
                        limit=10)
for obj in res.objects:
    print(obj.properties["title"])
client.close()

numericDrill.question: Dense ranks A 1st, B 2nd, C 3rd. Sparse ranks C 1st, A 2nd, D 3rd. With k = 60, which document wins RRF?
numericDrill.answer: A: 1/61 + 1/62 ≈ 0.03252. C: 1/63 + 1/61 ≈ 0.03226. A wins narrowly; B and D, found by only one method, trail.

interview.question: Why fuse by rank instead of raw scores?
interview.answer: Cosine and BM25 scores sit on different, query-dependent scales, so adding them is meaningless without normalization. RRF uses only ranks, which are comparable and robust.

interview.question: How do you enforce permissions in hybrid search?
interview.answer: Store access metadata (tenant, roles) with each chunk and filter inside the database before results leave it, ideally in both retrievers. Never rely on the LLM to hide content the user shouldn't see.

mistakes.mistake: Adding raw BM25 and cosine scores
mistakes.fix: Use RRF or normalize scores first

mistakes.mistake: Filtering permissions after the LLM sees results
mistakes.fix: Filter in the database before results are returned

quiz.question: Dense search ranks a runbook 1st and BM25 ranks it 4th. With k = 60, what is its RRF score?
Shoppers type “running shoe size 9 model 41”. Why does hybrid search help?
options: The query mixes intent with exact size and model tokens
The query is too long for embeddings
quiz.explanation: Dense search captures “running shoe”; BM25 matches “9” and “41” exactly.

quiz.question: Which are valid ways to combine dense and BM25 results? Select all that apply.
options: Normalise each score list, then weight with α
Add raw BM25 and cosine scores directly
Keep only the list whose top score is higher
quiz.explanation: Ranks or normalised scores are comparable. Raw BM25 and cosine scores sit on different scales.

quiz.question: What does raising the RRF constant k from 10 to 60 do?
options: Reduces the advantage of top ranks, so agreement across lists matters more
quiz.explanation: With k = 10, rank 1 beats rank 2 by 1/11 versus 1/12; with k = 60 the gap between 1/61 and 1/62 is much smaller.

quiz.question: A multi-hospital search must never show one hospital’s notes to another. Where should the tenant filter go?
options: In the prompt, asking the LLM to ignore other hospitals
Inside the database, in both retrievers, before results leave it
quiz.explanation: Permissions belong in the database query itself, never in the LLM or after ranking.

quiz.question: Document A is 1st in dense and absent from BM25. Document B is 3rd in dense and 2nd in BM25. With k = 60, which ranks higher?
Clients search for the ISIN “INE002A01018” and dense search returns unrelated funds. What is the fix?
options: Add BM25 and fuse the results
quiz.explanation: An ISIN is a rare exact token. Keyword search matches it; embeddings blur it.

quiz.question: Which are real pitfalls of hybrid search? Select all that apply.
options: Two indexes to keep in sync
Raw scores are not comparable across methods
Filtering after ranking can leave too few results
quiz.explanation: RRF needs no training; it only uses ranks.

quiz.question: After min–max normalisation a product has dense 0.8 and sparse 0.2. With α = 0.7 on dense, what is its fused score?
Filtering after fusion leaves 3 of 5 results on the page. Which fixes work? Select all that apply.
options: Oversample before filtering, for example fetch 50 and then filter
Use the vector database’s filter-aware search
quiz.explanation: Filtering first, or fetching enough extra candidates, keeps the page full. k does not change how many results survive.

quiz.question: In a Weaviate hybrid query, what does alpha = 0 mean?
quiz.explanation: In Weaviate, alpha = 1 is pure vector search and alpha = 0 is pure keyword search.

quiz.question: What is the default rank constant for reciprocal rank fusion in Elasticsearch?
quiz.explanation: Elasticsearch’s rank_constant defaults to 60, the value used in the original RRF paper.

quiz.question: How should you evaluate a hybrid search change? Select all that apply.
options: Use separate code-style and meaning-style query sets
Compare recall@k for dense, sparse and fused
Check that permission filters leave no leaks
Look only at the average cosine similarity of top results
quiz.explanation: Each method fails on different queries, and permissions must be tested too. Cosine averages say nothing about fused quality.

quiz.question: Travellers search for flight numbers such as “AI 302”. Which part of a hybrid system handles them best?
quiz.explanation: Exact identifiers are a sparse-retrieval strength.

quiz.question: Each retriever returns only its top 5 before fusion. What is the risk?
options: A document ranked 8th in both lists is never fused, although agreement would lift it
quiz.explanation: At rank 8 in both, RRF gives 2 ÷ 68 ≈ 0.029, more than a rank-1 hit in one list (≈ 0.016). Retrieve 50–100 from each.

quiz.question: Why does hybrid search often beat either method alone?
options: It doubles the number of vectors
Dense and sparse fail on different queries, so fusion combines their strengths
quiz.explanation: Dense handles paraphrases, sparse handles exact terms, and fusion keeps both.

quiz.question: Three retrievers rank a document 1st, 2nd and 3rd. With k = 60, what is its RRF score?
Where can tenant filters go safely in a hybrid pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: As a pre-filter inside the vector search
As a filter inside the keyword query
Applied by the LLM when it writes the answer
In both retrievers, using the same tenant metadata
quiz.explanation: Both retrievers must filter inside the database. The LLM is not an access-control layer.

quiz.question: A Postgres team wants hybrid search without adding a new database. What fits?
options: pgvector plus Postgres full-text search, fused with RRF in SQL
quiz.explanation: pgvector handles vectors and Postgres full-text search handles keywords; RRF is a few lines of SQL.

quiz.question: Weighted fusion works well on one query set and badly on another. Why?
options: RRF would need an α too
The best α depends on the query mix, so tune it on a representative evaluation set
quiz.explanation: Code-heavy queries want more sparse weight and paraphrases want more dense weight.
